A dog run built for a Pine Hills backyard

A Pine Hills dog run built in pet turf falls inside the published $10–$18-a-square-foot span, current as of September 2026, with $12–$16 covering most jobs. The community's older, wider 1960s and 1970s lots give a run more room than a newer subdivision yard typically spares, and a share of those same lots still route around a septic system's access point.

Reviewed by Luis Austin, owner · Last reviewed September 21, 2026

Room a newer subdivision lot doesn't have

A dog run competes for space on a small, newer lot in a way it usually doesn't on an older Pine Hills parcel, where a wider side yard or a deeper backyard leaves room for a run alongside a family lawn instead of replacing it. That extra width also means a run can be laid out as a long rectangle along a fence line rather than squeezed into an odd-shaped leftover corner, which is easier to keep dogs contained in and easier to drain evenly.

What a high water table does to a dog run in Pine Hills

Summer in Pine Hills pushes the water table close to the surface for weeks at a stretch, and a dog run sitting at grade on that kind of lot holds moisture from below as well as from rinsing on top. Raising the finished base slightly above the surrounding yard, using the fuller three- to four-inch depth the state's washed-rock standard allows, keeps a run above that saturation line instead of sitting in it during the wettest part of the year. Without that extra lift, a dog yard on low ground can smell and drain poorly even when the surface build above it was done correctly in every other respect.

Where a septic tank still sits under the yard

Most of Pine Hills still runs on individual septic systems outside the stretch of Pine Hills Road between Alhambra Drive and Golf Club Parkway that the county converted to sewer by June 2026 (the county’s septic-to-sewer project). On a lot that hasn't converted, the tank's pump-out lid has to stay reachable once a dog run or any other turf area is finished, which means mapping the system's layout before staking a run's corners, not after the base is already down.

Why a pet system needs a fully permeable backing

A plain residential lawn can use a semi-perforated backing and still meet the drainage requirement, but a Pine Hills pet system calls for a fully permeable version instead, since liquid needs a path through the backing itself, not just around scattered perforations. That distinction matters more with a dog in the yard than the backing material's brand or thickness does, because a backing with fewer or smaller openings can pass rainwater fine while still holding urine against the surface long enough to smell. Fully permeable backing paired with the deeper rock base underneath is what actually gets liquid moving down and away rather than pooling anywhere in between.

Say you have a 260 sq ft run behind a 1962 ranch home

Say you have a 260 sq ft dog run planned for the back fence line of a 1962 ranch home on a lot that hasn't yet converted from septic to county sewer. At $10–$18 per square foot, that run prices between $2,600 and $4,680, with most jobs like it landing in the $12–$16 typical band, or $3,120 to $4,160, once zeolite infill is added for odor control.

Because the property is still on septic, the crew locates the tank and drain field before finalizing the run's footprint, keeping the pump-out lid clear and shifting the layout a few feet if the original plan would have covered it.

The hose test a dog run gets before its first use

Once a Pine Hills dog run's last step of infill is brushed in, running a hose across the full footprint and watching where water goes is worth doing before a dog is ever let onto it, confirming the drain point actually clears standing water within roughly a minute the way the deeper base and permeable backing are built to. This test also surfaces any lingering odor from construction dust or adhesive before the run gets its first real use. Catching a slow spot on this walkthrough, while the crew is still on site, is simpler than tracing a smell back to a drainage issue weeks later.

The side-street swale a corner-lot run can end up inside

A Pine Hills corner lot commonly carries a drainage swale along its side-street frontage as well as its front one, and a dog run planned without checking that second boundary can end up partly inside a swale the state's rule flatly prohibits building turf inside, regardless of how convenient that stretch of yard looks for fencing. Because a run's footprint is usually smaller and more fixed by fence lines than an open lawn, discovering the conflict after fencing is already up means relocating the whole run rather than just pulling back one edge. Checking both frontages before staking the fence avoids that.

Capping a sprinkler zone that's older than the dog

A Pine Hills lot from the 1960s or 1970s often still runs on its original irrigation zones, sometimes patched or partially replaced over the decades but rarely redesigned from scratch. Before a dog run's turf goes in, whatever zone used to water that section gets capped at the valve, the same requirement that applies anywhere in Florida under the state's rule, and it's a good moment to check whether nearby zones still work at all before the rest of the yard gets attention later.

Clearing waste and debris so the base keeps draining

Solid waste left sitting on a Pine Hills dog run works down into the infill layer over time rather than staying on the surface, and once it's mixed in there, the same washed-rock base built to move liquid through quickly ends up working harder to do that job. Picking it up on a routine that doesn't lag more than a day or two, especially during the busiest summer stretch, keeps the base's percolation doing what it's designed for instead of fighting through material it was never meant to filter. This is one habit that matters more on a dedicated run than almost anywhere else on the property.

Questions people ask

Does a Pine Hills lot that already converted to sewer still need pump-out access planned?

No, not for that specific system. Once a parcel has switched from septic to county sewer, there's no tank left to keep reachable, though a neighboring lot that hasn't converted still needs that access point mapped before any turf goes in.

Is a weed barrier a good idea under a Pine Hills dog run?

Skip it specifically under the run. A layer of fabric between the base and the turf backing holds waste right at the surface rather than letting it pass down into the rock, fighting the fast drainage a dog run needs most. Elsewhere on the same lawn, the same fabric is fine, and optional.
